about: The mistakes small models repeat when they write Nuclear: each one cost a failed task in the evaluation. A row says the mistake, the right form and the kinds it applies to (`kinds`), so a coder reads the ones of the kind it is about to write.

rows.title: Pitfall: a decorator written after or beside its field
rows.summary: A decorator goes on the line right ABOVE the field or method it applies to, never after it and never on the same line. Written after, the compiler says `'@column' has no member below it` (`N0013`).
body: The same for a model's rules (`@minLength(2)` above `name: string`), a controller's routes (`@get("{id}")` above its method) and a test (`@test("...")` above its method).

rows.title: Pitfall: an application component with signatures or bodies
rows.summary: An `appcomponent` is only aliases to use cases: `name() = UseCase.exec`. Never a method signature, a body or constructor parameters. A signature alone is `N0221`.
body: // What the rest of the app sees of authors.
The alias takes the parameters and the result of the use case's `exec` by itself. On mobile and web the facade is `appcomponent BooksComponent`, written the same way.

rows.title: Pitfall: the kind word left out of the header
rows.summary: A declaration starts with its kind: `usecase FindBook(...)`, `repository BookRepository`, `controller BooksController(...)`, `listener BookEvents(...)`. Only where the folder gives the kind (models, state models) may the word be left out; when in doubt, write it.
body: Without its word the declaration is a plain module and nothing of its kind is generated for it. The task's own words are the kind: "a use case X" is `usecase X`, "an application component X" is `appcomponent X`.

rows.title: Pitfall: writing again the declarations the task only uses
rows.summary: Write only what the task declares. The files it depends on already exist: copying an entity, a repository or an example's other declarations into the new file declares them twice (`N0102`, `N0303`).
body: A task "a use case `BooksOfAuthor(books: BookRepository)`" is one declaration, the use case. `BookRepository` and `Book` are given as context so their names and members are known; they are not written again.

rows.title: Pitfall: a name, path or value changed from what the task says
rows.summary: Every name, decorator, path and value the task gives appears in the answer exactly as written. "Over the API's `books` path" is `@repository(path = "books")`; "at most 200 characters" is `@column(length = 200)`; a method the task calls `byAuthor` is not renamed.
body: A small model tends to tidy names (`getByAuthor`), to drop an option (`unique`) or to move a value to a comment. The acceptance checks look for the exact text, and so do the other pieces that call it.

rows.title: Pitfall: only the first of several declarations written
rows.summary: When the task names several declarations for one file (two models, a `state` and its `graph`), every one is written, one after another, each with its own doc comment.
body: // The fields of a book that may change.

rows.title: Pitfall: the library names of TypeScript, Dart or Python
rows.summary: The standard library is Nuclear's: `length` (a property), `add`, `addAll`, `remove`, `upper()`, `lower()`, `trim()`, `join`, `split`, `map`, `filter`, and `x in xs` for membership. `push`, `append`, `len(x)`, `toUpperCase`, `contains`, `includes` are `N0114`.
body: The compiler's message gives the Nuclear name, and `nuclear fix` writes it.

rows.title: Pitfall: `replace` where every occurrence must change
rows.summary: `replace(from, to)` changes only the first occurrence; `replaceAll(from, to)` changes every one.

rows.title: Pitfall: an asynchronous call used without `~`
rows.summary: A call to a repository, a use case, a facade's alias, an agent or a model is asynchronous: write `~` before it, once, and keep its value. Without it the value is not there yet (`N0222`).
body: A member right after the call needs parentheses: `(~books.byAuthor(author)).length`.

rows.title: Pitfall: a kept `Result` read as if it were its value
rows.summary: In a test (or any function that does not return a `Result`), `found = ~books.byId(1)` keeps the `Result`: read `found.isOk`, `found.value` and `found.error`, not `found.title` or `found.length`.

rows.title: Pitfall: a test that reads rows it never created
rows.summary: The databases are in memory and start empty in every test. A test first creates the rows it reads, through the code that adds them or `~repository.save(Entity(...))`, and only then checks.
body: A test that calls `~books.booksOf("Herbert")` and expects one book, without creating it first, fails with an empty list. Nothing of one test reaches the next.

rows.title: Pitfall: a test that injects a class the task does not name
rows.summary: Use only the declarations the task names. Never `inject<X>()` a class it does not list: copying a test of a close example brings classes of another project (`N0220`). When the task declares only models, build them and check their fields.

rows.title: Pitfall: a repository query that compares with a map of operators
rows.summary: A repository query compares with functions: `where({ "year": gte(year) })`, never `{ "year": { "gte": year } }`. The functions: `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `ne`, `like`, `ilike`, `oneOf`, `isNull`, `between`.
body: A method's lines build one query; the last line runs it (`getOne()`, `getMany()`, `paginate(page, size)`, `count()`, `exists()`).

rows.title: Pitfall: an HTTP repository method with a body
rows.summary: A repository over an API declares each request as a method WITHOUT a body, under `@repository(path = "books")`, with `@get(path = ":id")` (or `@post`, `@put`, `@patch`, `@delete`) above it. The framework makes the call.
body: `:id` takes the parameter `id`; the other parameters go to the query or the body.

rows.title: Pitfall: a state model written as fields, or with its manager in the same file
rows.summary: A state model is its name and ONE line with its states in parentheses; a boolean is a state without data. Nothing else goes in its file: no `statemanager`, no decorators, no methods.
body: That is the whole file. Each name in the parentheses is a state of the screen with the type of its data. The state manager that emits them is another file, in `managers/`, and another task.

rows.title: Pitfall: a graph node that does not end with its changes
rows.summary: In a `graph`, each node is a method that receives the state and whose LAST line is the map of what it changes, with the state's own field names as keys. `@next("other")` above a node names the node that runs AFTER it; the last node has `@next("end")`; the first has `@start`. A node never calls `run`.
body: // What a translation keeps between its steps.
// Translates a text in two steps.
- `first` is the first node (`@start`) and goes to `tidy` (`@next("tidy")` is above `first`).
- A node changes fields of the state by their own names (`rough`, `clean`); it invents no other key.
- When the task names the state and the graph, both are written in the file, the state first.
A graph of ONE node: that node is the first and the last, so it has both decorators and no other node is written:
Two nodes never have the same name.

rows.title: Pitfall: a use case with several methods, or whose `exec` returns a plain value
rows.summary: A `usecase` has exactly one method, `exec`, and it returns `Result<Error, T>`. A second operation is a second use case (`N0215`); a plain return type is `N0216`.
body: Errors of the business are returned, not thrown: `return Err(Conflict("${input.email} is taken"))`.

rows.title: Pitfall: named arguments written with a colon, or a constructor with `new`
rows.summary: A named argument is `name = value`: `Book(title = "Dune", year = 1965)`, `orderBy("year", desc = true)`. Not `title: "Dune"`, not `{ title }`, and never `new Book(...)`.
body: A map literal keeps its colons: `{ "author": author }`.

rows.title: Pitfall: braces, semicolons, `return` on the last line, `const`
rows.summary: Blocks are 2-space indentation, never braces; no semicolons; the last line of a function is its value (`return` only leaves early); a variable is declared by assigning it (`x = 1`); comments are `//`.

rows.title: Pitfall: a state manager without its state model, or with a method per state twice
rows.summary: A state manager has `@stateModel(State)` above it, its dependencies in the line under its name, and each method marked with the ONE state it emits (`@state(State.loaded)`). The error state is emitted by an `Err`: no method is written for it, and no method is declared twice.
body: The state model (`OrdersState`) is another file, in `state_models/`: it is not written here.

rows.title: Pitfall: the status of a route written inside its method
rows.summary: The status a route answers is part of its decorator, above the method: `@post("{bookId}", status = 201)`. A `@post` already answers 201 and the others 200. A decorator is never written inside a method's body or after its last line.
body: place(productId: int, buyer: string) Result<Error, Order>
The body of a route is only its call to the component's facade, awaited with `~`.
